common_name: Nachtigall Hydrangea (Teller Series Deep Blue-Violet Lacecap)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in rich, moist, well-drained soil with afternoon shade and some shelter from wind; Nachtigall is a 1979 release from the Swiss Teller breeding program in Wadenswil, bred from the same ('Mowe' x 'Glarnisch') x ('Bodensee' x 'Enziandom') cross that produced 'Blaumeise' and 'Eisvogel'.

directions: Nachtigall is a Teller-series lacecap bred at the Swiss federal horticultural research station in Wadenswil, named like its siblings 'Blaumeise', 'Taube', and 'Fasan' for a songbird. Its flat lacecap heads trend strongly toward deep royal blue in acidic soil, shifting to violet or occasional dark pink where soil is more alkaline. It is a vigorous, strong-stemmed grower that can reach shrub-sized proportions where winters are mild, but it is less cold-hardy than many macrophylla cultivars and benefits from a sheltered site with afternoon shade. Prune only right after flowering, since buds for next year's bloom form on the current season's old wood over summer.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society) — Hydrangea Section Macrophyllae Cultivars N–O
Heritage Hydrangeas Nursery — Hydrangea macrophylla Nachtigall
Hortensias du Haut-Bois — Nachtigall

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Westfalen was introduced in 1940 by German breeder Joseph Wintergalen and has remained in cultivation as a reliably compact red-pink mophead.

directions: Westfalen is one of the older German mophead cultivars still grown today, dating to 1940, and is prized for staying dense and compact, rarely topping about three and a half feet on strong, thick stems that resist flopping under heavy flower heads. Entire-edged sepals hold a strong red-pink color that leans toward purple rather than true blue even on acidic soil, distinguishing it from blue-trending German cultivars like 'Nachtigall' or 'Blaumeise'. It is sometimes compared to the similarly red-toned 'Ami Pasquier', though Westfalen stays noticeably smaller and tighter in habit. Plant in moist, humus-rich soil with afternoon shade, and limit pruning to right after bloom to protect next year's old-wood flower buds.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society) — Hydrangea Section Macrophyllae Cultivars V–Z
American Hydrangea Society

common_name: Dear Dolores Hydrangea (Southern Living Collection Large Blue-to-Pink Mophead)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Dear Dolores (patented as 'Wyatt LeFever') is a Southern Living Plant Collection selection bred for an especially large, reblooming mophead habit.

directions: Dear Dolores grows noticeably larger than many modern reblooming mopheads, reaching around five feet tall and wide at maturity, and produces rounded flower heads that shift blue in acidic soil and pink in alkaline soil. It flowers on both old and new wood, opening a first flush in spring followed by continued summer and fall bloom, so winter dieback or a late freeze does not erase the whole season's display. Give it consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, with protection from hot afternoon sun in warmer zones. Because of its larger mature size, allow extra room compared with compact series hydrangeas when siting it in a mixed border.
sources: Southern Living Plant Collection — Dear Dolores Hydrangea

common_name: Let's Dance Arriba Hydrangea (Compact Reblooming Violet-to-Pink Mophead)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Let's Dance Arriba is a Proven Winners reblooming hydrangea bred from a macrophylla x serrata cross for improved cold hardiness and prolific bloom.

directions: Let's Dance Arriba is among the hardiest and most prolific bloomers in the Let's Dance series, rated to USDA zone 4 thanks to its macrophylla x serrata parentage. Dense, mophead-type flower heads open rich violet-purple in acidic soil and saturated pink in more alkaline soil, aging to a soft mauve late in the season. It flowers on both old and new wood, so plants keep blooming through summer and fall even after a hard winter damages the previous year's stems. Grow in part sun to full sun in cooler climates, shifting toward more afternoon shade where summers run hot, in consistently moist, well-drained soil.
sources: Proven Winners ColorChoice — Let's Dance Arriba Reblooming Hydrangea

common_name: Let's Dance Big Band Hydrangea (Compact Large-Flowered Reblooming Mophead)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Let's Dance Big Band is a Proven Winners reblooming bigleaf hydrangea selected for extra-large flower heads on a tidy, rounded two-and-a-half-foot plant.

directions: Let's Dance Big Band stands out in the Let's Dance series for unusually large flower heads that emerge early in vivid pink or purple on a compact, rounded plant only about two and a half feet tall and wide. It reblooms on both old and new wood through summer and into fall, and flower color follows soil pH, leaning blue in acidic soil and pink in neutral to alkaline soil. Plant in full sun to part sun with consistently moist, well-drained soil, giving afternoon shade in hot-summer regions. Prune lightly to shape after the first flush rather than hard, since old-wood buds set the bulk of the display.
sources: Proven Winners ColorChoice — Let's Dance Big Band Reblooming Bigleaf Hydrangea

common_name: Let's Dance Blue Jangles Hydrangea (Compact Reblooming Blue-to-Pink Lacecap)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Let's Dance Blue Jangles is a Proven Winners reblooming lacecap hydrangea notable for a tight, compact habit unusual among old-and-new-wood bloomers.

directions: Let's Dance Blue Jangles carries bold lacecap flowers with a ring of showy sterile florets around the fertile center, opening from early summer into early fall on both old and new wood. Color shifts with soil chemistry, reading as rich blue or purple in acidic soil and pink in alkaline soil, with pink overtones often appearing at the branch tips regardless of overall hue. Unlike many lacecap types that sprawl, this selection keeps an unusually tight, compact three-foot habit, making it useful for foundation plantings and smaller borders. Grow in partial shade with consistently moist, well-drained soil, and prune only lightly right after the main flush of bloom.
sources: Proven Winners ColorChoice — Let's Dance Blue Jangles Reblooming Bigleaf Hydrangea

common_name: Let's Dance Can Do Hydrangea (Continuous-Blooming Reblooming Lacecap)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Let's Dance Can Do is a Proven Winners macrophylla x serrata hybrid bred to flower continuously from its first year in the garden.

directions: Let's Dance Can Do was bred as a breakthrough continuous bloomer, producing lacecap flowers from strawberry pink to lavender to baby blue depending on soil pH almost nonstop through the growing season, even on young plants in their first year. Its macrophylla x serrata heritage gives it better cold hardiness than most bigleaf hydrangeas, rated to USDA zone 4, and it flowers reliably on new growth when winter damages old wood. Plant in part sun to full sun with consistently moist, well-drained soil; more sun generally means more flowers, provided roots stay cool and hydrated. Deadhead spent flower heads to keep the continuous-bloom habit tidy, but avoid hard pruning that removes developing buds.
sources: Proven Winners ColorChoice — Let's Dance Can Do Reblooming Mountain Hydrangea

common_name: Let's Dance Lovable Hydrangea (2026 Hydrangea of the Year Reblooming Mophead)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Let's Dance Lovable is a Proven Winners reblooming mophead hydrangea named the 2026 Hydrangea of the Year.

directions: Let's Dance Lovable produces large mophead flower heads in rich royal purple to blue on acidic soil or warm, saturated pink on basic soil, blooming from early summer through fall on both old and new wood. Foliage turns burgundy in fall, adding a second season of color after bloom winds down. Plant in part sun in southern climates, moving toward part to full sun farther north, spacing plants three to four feet apart in consistently moist, well-drained soil. Protect from harsh winter damage where possible, but expect reliable rebloom on new wood even after a rough winter or mistimed pruning.
sources: Proven Winners ColorChoice — Let's Dance Hydrangeas

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Grayswood is a British garden selection valued as one of the taller, later-blooming members of the Hydrangea serrata group.

directions: Grayswood is one of the larger, more vigorous mountain hydrangeas, growing taller than most of its serrata relatives and reaching shrub-sized proportions where conditions suit it. Lacecap flower heads open with a center of small blue (or pink, depending on soil pH) fertile florets ringed by white sterile florets, and the whole head gradually flushes to crimson red as the season progresses, continuing from midsummer into fall. Foliage follows a similar seasonal shift, with pale and darker green leaves developing reddish-brown tips in late summer and fall. Grow in partial shade with consistently moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil, pruning only lightly right after flowering to protect next year's old-wood buds.
sources: JC Raulston Arboretum Plant Database — Hydrangea serrata Grayswood
Secret Garden Growers — Hydrangea serrata Grayswood

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to light shade; Yae-no-amacha is a traditional Japanese mountain hydrangea selection whose name translates roughly to 'double-flowered sweet tea hydrangea', referencing the amacha tea brewed from serrata leaves.

directions: Yae-no-amacha is a Japanese mountain hydrangea whose lacecap heads carry single to double sterile florets, giving the flowers a fuller, more layered look than a typical single-row lacecap. Color ranges from pale pink to lavender-blue depending on soil pH, and the plant blooms over a long stretch nearly all summer. It stays compact for a mountain hydrangea, reaching roughly three feet tall by four feet wide after about a decade, and tolerates more shade than most bigleaf hydrangeas, thriving from partial sun to fairly deep shade. Plant in humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil, and prune lightly right after bloom since flower buds form on the prior season's wood.
sources: Mr. Maple — Hydrangea serrata Yae-no-amacha Mountain Hydrangea
Forestfarm Nursery — Hydrangea serrata Yae no Amacha

common_name: Seaside Serenade Fire Island Hydrangea (Reblooming White-to-Red-Edged Mophead)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Fire Island is a member of the Seaside Serenade series of reblooming bigleaf hydrangeas bred for a tidy habit and long-season color-shifting mophead blooms.

directions: Fire Island opens with white mophead flowers ringed in rosy red, then gradually ages first to deeper pink and finally to a soft ivory as the blooms mature, giving a single flower head multiple looks over its lifespan. Like the rest of the Seaside Serenade series, it flowers on both old and new wood, so a late frost or hard winter does not eliminate the season's display. Grow in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, with protection from hot afternoon sun in warmer regions. Deadhead as blooms fade to encourage continued flowering, and prune lightly right after the main flush rather than hard in winter.
sources: Monrovia — Seaside Serenade Hydrangea Collection

common_name: Seaside Serenade Glacier Bay Hydrangea (Compact Black-Stemmed White Lacecap)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Glacier Bay is a member of the Seaside Serenade series selected for crisp white lacecap flowers set off by dramatic near-black stems.

directions: Glacier Bay stands out in the Seaside Serenade series for pure white lacecap flower heads held above dark, nearly black stems, a contrast that remains striking regardless of soil pH since the white color does not shift with acidity the way pink and blue cultivars do. It reblooms on both old and new wood from summer into fall and keeps a compact, dense habit around three feet tall and wide, with bright green, thick foliage. Grow in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, giving afternoon protection from hot sun. Light pruning right after the main bloom flush helps maintain shape without sacrificing next season's old-wood buds.

common_name: Seaside Serenade Crystal Cove Hydrangea (Reblooming Deep Purple-Blue-to-Pink Lacecap)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Crystal Cove is a member of the Seaside Serenade series bred for intensely saturated lacecap color that holds up well through the season.

directions: Crystal Cove carries lacecap flower heads in an unusually deep, saturated purple-blue in acidic soil, shifting to an equally rich deep pink where soil runs more alkaline. Like other Seaside Serenade members, it reblooms on both old and new wood, extending color from early summer well into fall. Grow in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, with protection from hot afternoon sun in warmer climates, and consider aluminum sulfate soil amendments to intensify or hold the blue end of its color range. Deadhead spent heads to encourage continued bloom and limit pruning to right after the first flush.

common_name: Seaside Serenade Cape May Hydrangea (Compact Reblooming Blue-to-Pink Lacecap)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Cape May is a compact member of the Seaside Serenade series grown for classic blue-to-pink lacecap flowers on a tidy, three-foot plant.

directions: Cape May produces classic flat lacecap flower heads that read blue in acidic soil and pink in alkaline soil, on a compact plant that stays around three feet tall and wide, making it a good fit for smaller borders and foundation plantings where larger Seaside Serenade members would crowd the space. It flowers on both old and new wood, continuing to bloom through summer and fall even after winter dieback. Grow in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, and amend with aluminum sulfate or garden lime to nudge color toward blue or pink as desired. Prune lightly right after the first bloom flush to preserve old-wood flower buds.

common_name: Seaside Serenade Martha's Vineyard Hydrangea (Reblooming Pink-Red Mophead)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Martha's Vineyard is a member of the Seaside Serenade series grown for dense pink-red mophead clusters on a three- to four-foot plant.

directions: Martha's Vineyard produces full, rounded mophead flower heads in strong pink-red tones, reblooming on both old and new wood to extend color from early summer into fall. It grows into a fuller-sized shrub than some of the series' most compact members, reaching three to four feet tall and wide. Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, with afternoon shade in hot climates to prevent flower and leaf scorch. Deadhead as blooms fade and limit pruning to right after the main flush, since next year's flowers set on the current season's old wood.

common_name: Seaside Serenade Newport Hydrangea (Reblooming Deep Plum-to-Pink Mophead)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Newport is a member of the Seaside Serenade series notable for unusually deep plum flower color in acidic soil.

directions: Newport's mophead flower heads take on an unusually deep, moody plum color in acidic soil, shifting to a vibrant, more conventional pink where soil is alkaline, offering a richer color range than many series relatives. It reblooms on both old and new wood from summer through fall, growing into a rounded three- to four-foot shrub. Grow in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, and amend soil pH deliberately if a particular plum or pink tone is the goal. Deadhead spent flower heads and prune only lightly right after the first bloom flush.

common_name: Seaside Serenade Cape Lookout Hydrangea (Reblooming White-to-Soft-Pink Mophead)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Cape Lookout is a member of the Seaside Serenade series grown for soft white-to-pink mophead flowers on a compact three-and-a-half-foot plant.

directions: Cape Lookout opens with clean white mophead flowers that gradually age to a soft, gentle pink, a color progression that holds fairly steady regardless of soil pH compared with the blue-to-pink shifts typical of most bigleaf hydrangeas. It reblooms on both old and new wood through summer and fall on a compact plant around three and a half feet tall and three feet wide. Grow in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, with protection from hot afternoon sun. Deadhead as flowers age past their peak and prune lightly right after the main bloom flush.

common_name: Seaside Serenade Outer Banks Hydrangea (Reblooming Blue-to-Pink Lacecap)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Outer Banks is the largest-growing lacecap in the Seaside Serenade series, reaching about four feet tall and wide.

directions: Outer Banks is among the larger-growing members of the Seaside Serenade series, reaching about four feet tall and wide, with flat lacecap flower heads that read blue in acidic soil and pink in alkaline soil. It reblooms on both old and new wood, giving a long season of color from summer into fall and resilience against winter stem loss. Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, with afternoon shade where summers are hot. Prune lightly right after the first bloom flush rather than hard in winter, to protect the buds that form on older wood.
